about.title: About Carburetor CFM Calculator
about.description: The Carburetor CFM Calculator determines the correct carburetor airflow capacity (CFM) for your engine based on displacement, RPM, and modification level. This professional engine airflow sizing tool is essential for proper carburetor sizing and optimal engine performance. Proper carburetor sizing ensures optimal air-fuel mixture delivery, preventing lean or rich conditions that can damage engines or reduce performance. This calculator helps match carburetor capacity to engine requirements for stock and modified engines.

faq.q: What happens if my carburetor CFM is too small for my engine?
faq.a: A carburetor with insufficient CFM restricts airflow, causing lean air-fuel ratios, power loss, and potential engine damage. The engine won't reach its full performance potential, especially at higher RPMs. Use our carburetor CFM calculator to determine the correct sizing for optimal performance.

faq.q: Can a carburetor be too big for my engine displacement?
faq.a: Yes, an oversized carburetor can cause poor idle quality, reduced low-end torque, and difficulty tuning. It's generally better to be slightly undersized than oversized for street applications. Our calculator helps find the optimal CFM range for your specific engine.

faq.q: How does engine modification level affect carburetor CFM requirements?
faq.a: Modified engines with performance camshafts, headers, intake manifolds, and higher compression ratios need more CFM due to improved breathing capacity and higher RPM capability. Modified engines typically require 15-20% more CFM than stock configurations.

faq.q: What's the difference between primary and secondary CFM in carburetors?
faq.a: Primary CFM handles idle and low-speed operation through the primary barrels, while secondary CFM provides additional airflow for high-RPM performance through secondary barrels. Total carburetor CFM is the sum of both primary and secondary ratings.

faq.q: How do I calculate CFM requirements for my engine displacement?
faq.a: Use the formula: (Displacement × RPM × Volumetric Efficiency) ÷ 3456 = CFM. For stock engines, use 1.5 CFM per cubic inch. For modified engines, use 1.8-2.0 CFM per cubic inch. Our calculator automates this process for accuracy.

faq.q: Which carburetor brands work best with calculated CFM requirements?
faq.a: Popular brands like Holley, Edelbrock, Demon, and Quick Fuel all offer carburetors in various CFM ratings. Choose based on your calculated CFM needs, budget, and intended use (street, strip, or racing applications).
